body_markdown: Palm trees, pastels, bikinis, fast boats—the mood of *Miami Vice* captured the essence of the era in the bright and fashionable South Florida city. Producer Michael Mann’s hit series starring Don Johnson as Sonny Crockett and Philip Michael Thomas as Rico Tubbs debuted on NBC in 1984 and quickly became appointment television on Friday nights. And for its first two seasons, *Miami Vice* also served as the ideal free advertisement for McBurnie Coachcraft, the small firm behind the black California Daytona Spyder at the heart of the show. But how, exactly, did it get there? Universal City Studios ## Origins of the *Miami Vice* California Daytona Spyder Southern California car designer Tom McBurnie began crafting vehicles from fiberglass in the 1970s as part of the Sceptre Motorcar Company.[The firm’s 6.6S](https://www.clenetclub.com/the-sceptre-66s-gallery.html) , a low-volume neoclassic in the art deco style of a prewar French car, won Best of Show at the 1978 Los Angeles Auto Show. On the heels of his early success, exotic car dealer Al Mardikian approached McBurnie to create a Cobra replica. Mardikian ran an impressive high-end showroom in Newport Beach called Trend Import Sales, which largely traded in “gray market” cars from Europe. His idea for the Cobra was to create a fiberglass replica body, put it on an American chassis, and sell it through the dealership. McBurnie’s bid for the Cobra project was about the same price as other proposals, and Mardikian went a different direction. But the rejection sparked a new idea for McBurnie, fueled by one particular car that was sitting in the dealership at the time. “When I walked into his showroom, there was a white Ferrari 365 GTS/4 Daytona Spider,” McBurnie says. “I had to walk past that to go to his office.” Despite losing the bid to construct the Cobra, McBurnie was quick to save the meeting. “Why don’t you do a Daytona?” he asked. Mardikian bought into the idea and the project was a go. ## The Ferrari Daytona Story Broad Arrow Ferrari SpA From 1969 to 1973, Ferrari built 1284 copies of the 365 GTB/4. In the nomenclature, 365 represented the volume in cubic centimeters of each of the engine’s 12 cylinders, GTB stood for Grand Touring Berlinetta (coupe), and the 4 indicated the total number of camshafts. Simultaneously, Carrozzeria Scaglietti produced 122 open variants—known as the 365 GTS/4—S for Spider, spelled as such because Italian lacks the letter “y”. The press, however, nicknamed the cars “Daytona” to commemorate the Ferrari’s 1-2-3 victory 18 months prior at the 1967 24 Hours of Daytona, which actually had nothing to do with the 365 GTB/4 itself. Ferrari never officially adopted the moniker, but it stuck. By the early ’80s, the rarity and desirability of the Spiders had sent their values climbing relative to their closed siblings (approximately $50K vs. $30K), and a cottage industry evolved around converting coupes to Spiders. Among the firms that performed the work to covert a Berlinetta to a Spider were Autosport in Modena, Autokraft in the U.K., the Richard Straman Company in Costa Mesa, California, and Michael Sheehan’s European Auto Restoration, also in Costa Mesa. These shops, plus a few others, created around 100 vehicles, which became known as “cut cars.” This Spider conversion by the Richard Straman Company was sold by Mecum in Monterey 2023 for $671K. Mecum Some conversions were better performed and more authentic-looking than others. The factory cars had structural changes incorporated to account for the lack of a fixed roof, along with the replacement of fiberglass components with sheetmetal (including front inner fenders and interior front and rear bulkheads) to improve rigidity. Most cut cars lacked these additional modifications. Today, factory Spiders in #2 (excellent) condition are closer to[$2.3M](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/365_gts!!4/1971/1971-ferrari-365_gts!!4-daytona?id=aCn1I000000CsT2SAK&condition=excellent) vs.[$640K](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/365_gtb!!4/1969/1969-ferrari-365_gtb!!4-daytona?id=aCn1I000000DEoHSAW&condition=excellent) for a #2 Berlinetta, while cut cars in similar shape sell for around[$500K](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/365_gtb!!4/1969/1969-ferrari-365_gtb!!4-daytona?id=aCn1I000000DTExSAO&condition=excellent) . ## Replicating the Daytona “Ferrari parts” listed in the McBurnie brochure included park light and tailight lenses, license light, quarter bumpers, and grille. This car had a set of the 16-inch diameter five-spoke modular wheels in silver. The options allowed buyers to have a personalized California Daytona Spyder different from the TV car. McBurnie Coachcraft McBurnie’s pitch to Mardikian, however, was something else entirely—a Daytona Spider replica. “He gave me the Daytona,” McBurnie says. “I had it for a little over a year. Mardikian also gave him a 1976 Corvette to build his replica around. “I took all the parts off of the Daytona, so I could see the body shape.” It had a 94.5-inch wheelbase. He also deconstructed the Corvette. “The first thing I did was measure the frame, the width of the windshield, the wheelbase.” Although the Corvette’s wheelbase was 98 inches, it wasn’t all that far off. And while there were a few other minor measurement differences, nothing indicated to McBurnie this was an undoable, far-fetched challenge. “Next, I sketched what was going to happen on the Corvette. I made fiberglass parts, put them on the Corvette and started bonding. Mr. Mardikian wanted the car to be very close to the original. He provided to me the Ferrari’s external parts—bumpers, taillights, grille, side marker lights, the complete (front) side marker light assembly. I made all those fit and I made the body panels.“ The car took McBurnie more than a year to build; given the slight differences between the Daytona and the Corvette, the modifications to the body had to be made with utmost care so that the original Pininfarina body design was not compromised. But the build project was a success. The car looked proportional, with the extra length of the Corvette chassis built into the area between the front cowl and front wheel opening. McBurnie incorporated small, tasteful wheel flares into the design, and the end result was very well received. “I got it to the ‘ready to paint’ stage and delivered that to Albert. He took it to a paint shop, it was painted dark Ferrari Red, and it was introduced as the Mardikian 350 GTS.” ## Spyder Casting Call The *Miami Vice* hero car on the set of the season 1 episode “One-Eyed Jack.” NBCUniversal via Getty Images McBurnie built four cars in all for Mardikian. To celebrate, McBurnie says Mardikian hosted a Newport Beach to-do. “Albert had this ‘coming out party’ for his Mardikian 350 GTS. He invited all the people that were customers of his car to the Balboa Bay Club.” One of those customers was Dan Haggerty, who had played the titular character in the film and TV series *The Life and Times of Grizzly Adams* . Preproduction on *Miami Vice* was already underway and, McBurnie says, “Haggerty knew either Michael Mann or the people in transportation who were looking for cars. He was the man who told them about the Daytona that I had built, the Mardikian 350.” Universal Studios ultimately leased two of these creations from Mardikian—a hero car and a stunt car. The show aired as a two-hour pilot on September 16, 1984, and viewers not only got their first glimpse of a new, more cinematic style of television production, they came face to face with McBurnie’s creation—most notably in single, nearly dialogue-free driving scene set to Phil Collins’ “In the Air Tonight.” And based on the show’s immediate success, Universal soon purchased both examples. The near-instant exposure gained from *Miami Vice* launched McBurnie’s business for what he began calling the California Daytona Spyder. “I had shown a couple cars and was building three or four cars when *Miami Vice* came out,” he says. “It was crazy, orders from everybody! I built 92 complete cars, including the four for Albert. And I built a little over 350 kits. *Miami Vice* was good advertising for me—the hottest TV program at the time.” McBurnie customers came up with their color choices, and red and black were the most popular by far. Some customers chose actual Ferrari paint code hues, including Fly Yellow, all to give these fiberglass-bodied creations a certain Ferrari flavor. James Maxwell One design element that differentiates the McBurnie car from a genuine Ferrari Daytona are the small flares on the wheel arches, with the lip continuing to the full width of the lower front valance. Amber-hued Ferrari parking light lenses provided great eye appeal on the front end, complete with “Prancing Horse” insignia. James Maxwell James Maxwell At times when multiple CDS cars were finished and waiting for customers to pick up, there were excellent opportunities to capture them on film, like here at the Gillespie Field Airport, located directly across the road from the McBurnie’s Santee, CA, shop. James Maxwell Not all the McBurnie turn-key customers that opted for black car were trying to duplicate the TV car. In the case of this example, Monocoque Wheels did up special gold-center three-piece wheels with “McBurnie” logos on one of the five spokes, and spinner center caps were added. When Tom McBurnie designed the car, he chose readily available Alfa Romeo Spider door handles, giving an Italian flavor. James Maxwell Not all the cars were painted black, red, or yellow! This customer opted for a metallic silver hue, complete with matching gray Connolly leather interior. James Maxwell Standard Corvette convertible roof mechanisms were used, and the overall appearance with the top up seems to fit the body style, while not screaming “Corvette” in any way. The black California Daytona Spyder is along side another McBurnie Coachcraft car available at the time, the Ferrari GTO-themed Datsun Z. James Maxwell “Create your own Friday night excitement” was the way McBurnie Coachcraft promoted the car on this display board, featuring a picture McBurnie snapped of one of the early cars on the sands of Pacific Beach in San Diego. [Bryan Gerould](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bryan-gerould/) When *Autobuff* magazine requested the car for a layout in its pages, a customer car was made available, done in a dark red hue and Zenith wire wheels, and this one sported Ferrari emblems. James Maxwell Red was clearly a popular color for the cars. Wire wheels (with spinners rather than standard five-lug attachment) were fitted on this one, and the owner went with black rear view mirrors rather than body color, and also chose saddle tan Connolly leather upholstery. While there are no actual Ferrari emblems on the body itself, the spinners have yellow center markings with Ferrari prancing horses and the front parking lenses have small prancing horse markings in black. James Maxwell Of course, *Miami Vice* was a huge talking point for McBurnie when selling his kits. If a home builder had a 1968–82 Corvette—either a complete car or even a wrecked one without frame damage—and was willing to perform the DIY work, then they’d end up with California Daytona Spyder that looked like the one Don Johnson drove on Friday nights, all for a reasonable price. The kits required only basic body shop skills, and most buyers would then find an upholstery shop for the leather work. Rare Corvettes, or anything viewed as “collectible,” like 1968–69 427 cars, LT1 small-block cars, or ’78 Silver Anniversary cars, weren’t typical donors. The wood-rimmed three-spoke steering wheel reveals the Corvette’s cross-flagged logo, and GM’s ignition key on the steering column is a dead giveaway of the origins of the car. The dash design came from McBurnie and was given a European flavor while retaining the Corvette gauges. James Maxwell When a “turn-key” CDS was built, the owner specified the powerplant, based on desired horsepower and expected drivability characteristics. Here’s a popular choice from that era: The “TPI” V-8 was the flagship performance engine for Chevrolet in the 1980s. This powerplant was known around Chevrolet dealerships as the L98 and featured “Elephant Trunk” intake runners, was rated at 245 horsepower stock, and had extra potential with more aggressive camshafts, larger throttle bodies, and head porting. James Maxwell This exploded-view drawing shows the various components of the hand-laid fiberglass body and related pieces as part of the California Daytona Spyder kit. Home builders did need to have some basic body shop skills, and to help them with the build a detailed assembly manual came with it. The early bodies were two-piece, with the sections meeting at the rocker panels; later came the one-piece body, designed to quicken building time. McBurnie Coachcraft Beyond the show, McBurnie’s California Daytona Spyders gained automotive media exposure as well. *Motor Trend* and various Corvette magazines gave coverage, one was invited to be on display at the SEMA Show in Las Vegas, and they also appeared at huge kit car events, including the Knott’s Berry Farm gathering. In an era when kit cars were the rage, for a brief time, the California Daytona Spyder was king. Kits were priced at $8000 (about $25,000 today), with turn-key cars $39,000 (about $121,000 today) and up, depending on equipment and performance enhancements. Business boomed, and turn-key cars were always in process at the shop. There were also people who bought McBurnie’s kits and then copied everything in order to start their own companies making Daytona knock-offs. There is, of course, some irony in that… ## The Beginning of the End McBurnie Coachcraft Two seasons of *Miami Vice* had aired before the proverbial wheels fell off McBurnie’s California Daytona Spyders. In 1986, Ferrari SpA, of Modena, Italy, filed a lawsuit against McBurnie Coachcraft, No. 86-1812-B, under the legal precedent of trade dress protection. Ferrari argued McBurnie’s cars were illegal copies that could cause the general public to confuse them for the real thing and cheapen the Italian carmaker’s image. At the time, Fiat was half-owner of Ferrari, so it was like a modern-day David vs. Goliath in a sense, an automotive giant going after a small car-building shop in the San Diego area. “We build high-quality cars, we’re low production, and I don’t see how a small company like ourselves could ruin a multinational conglomerate like Fiat,” McBurnie told a news outlet at the time. Rather, he compared his reproduction (turn-key) cars to the lithographs of great art masterpieces, having the effect of enhancing the value of the original. In the[final 1989 decision](https://web.archive.org/web/20260610211902/https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1989/05/18/ferrari-victory-forces-end-to-daytona-spyder-replicar/) , a jury of five men and one woman sided with Ferrari, calling the Daytona Spider “unique and distinctive,” and McBurnie was ordered to cease all production. *Miami Vice* , of course, soldiered on for another three seasons, but it was the end of the road for the California Daytona Spyder’s starring role. A legal agreement between Ferrari and the show’s producers in 1986, ahead of the show’s third season, mandated the replica be removed from production. But as a show of good will, Ferrari agreed to provide two new Testarossas (real ones), which arrived wearing black paint; they were repainted white to better show in the after-dark scenes. To write McBurnie’s replica out of the series, the Season 3 premiere featured an arms dealer who blew up Crockett’s Daytona (a fake one, and not even one of the McBurnie “fakes,” but a stationary prop) with a Stinger missile. Problem solved! Still, there’s an argument to be made that the black Daytona remains a favorite with many fans of the series. McBurnie’s[California Daytona Spyders](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/ferrari-365-daytona-spyder-replica/) do[pop up](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/ferrari-daytona-spyder-replica/) from[time to time](https://bringatrailer.com/listing/ferrari-daytona-replica/) at online auctions, mostly the completed kits, and with prices ranging from $25,000 to $50,000. By comparison, in the last year, four real 365 GTS/4 Daytona Spiders have traded at auction, for $2.27M–$2.53M. The record sale price, meanwhile, was achieved by RM Sotheby’s at its 2024 Monaco sale, for[chassis](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/mc24/lots/r0111-1972-ferrari-365-gts4-daytona-spider-by-scaglietti/)[15383](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/mc24/lots/r0111-1972-ferrari-365-gts4-daytona-spider-by-scaglietti/) , the 1972 Spider shown below, which brought €3.4M ($3.7M). RM Sotheby's/Stephan Bauer RM Sotheby's/Stephan Bauer RM Sotheby's/Stephan Bauer RM Sotheby's/Stephan Bauer Following their exit from the series, the two cars used in filming reportedly went to a fellow named Carl Roberts, who in exchange provided the show with a Testarossa stunt car built from a DeTomaso Pantera. One of the Spyders next appeared in 1989, in the third installment of *Cannonball Run* , which is known by various titles, including *Speed Zone* , starring John Candy. Today, one car is said to be in a private collection, while the other has been displayed at various auto museums, including the Volo Auto Museum in Illinois and, currently, the Petersen Automotive Museum in Los Angeles. Quad rectangular headlights covered by clear Plexiglas, wire wheels and black paint, saddle tan leather upholstery, Corvette-based dashboard, Momo three-spoke leather-wrapped steering wheel, rectangular rear view mirrors—all part of the “TV car” appearance formula. Petersen Automotive Museum Florida Dade County “ZAQ 178” 1984 license plate as used on the show. This car was based on a 1981 Corvette. It’s an unrestored car and as it appeared on the show. This #4 car was loaned to the museum’s exhibit from a private collector who had obtained it back in 1988. Petersen Automotive Museum Tom McBurnie had made an appearance at the Volo Museum to greet car owners and enthusiasts and answer questions about the cars and his design work. Volo Museum This #1 car was based on a 1976 Corvette and was used for driving and stunt scenes, fitted with camera rigging mounts, skids, and a special stunt brake. The car has seen a full restoration and is on permanent display at the Volo Museum in Volo, Illinois. Volo Museum Earlier this year, Tom McBurnie was invited to Jay Leno’s Garage with one of the cars, though the episode isn’t out yet. Old episodes of *Miami Vice* are, however, and you can stream them in the usual places, free with ads or for a nominal fee, which is a great opportunity to introduce the groundbreaking show to people who missed the original airing, and to bring back the broad spectrum of memories for those who were captivated by it in the ’80s. Michael Mann reprised the Crockett and Tubbs duo for a 2006 film, starring Colin Farrell and Jamie Foxx, and for fans both old and new, a stylized reboot, *Miami Vice ’85,* is in the works, starring Michael B. Jordan, Austin Butler, and John Leguizamo. It is slated for 2028 release and is said to be a throwback to the original TV presentation, taking inspiration from the show’s pilot episode and first season. The big question for gearheads, of course, will surround the hero car: Might we see a real 365 GTS/4 this go-round?
